name: Gutenberg Bible
info: The Gutenberg Bible, also called the 42-line Bible, is an edition of the Latin Vulgate printed by Johannes Gutenberg at Mainz in the 1450s, the earliest major book printed in Europe with mass-produced metal movable type.

facts.made: Johannes Gutenberg, printer, at Mainz in the Holy Roman Empire; the text is the Vulgate, the Latin translation of St Jerome, with emendations from the Parisian Bible tradition
facts.form: A Latin Bible in blackletter type, usually bound in two volumes, with 1,288 pages in a complete copy, 42 lines to the page, on paper or vellum; a full sheet of Royal paper measures 42 cm by 60 cm
facts.where: 49 copies survive in at least substantial portion, mostly in university libraries and other scholarly institutions, among them three at the Morgan Library and Museum in New York; fragments are held in many other libraries
facts.known: The earliest major book printed in Europe with mass-produced metal movable type; the 42-line page; an oil-based ink; hand rubrication and illumination; the 1455 letter of the future Pius II; the high prices of its surviving copies; its place in the Gutenberg Revolution

t: Gutenberg printed the Vulgate at Mainz in the 1450s with mass-produced metal type, in a run that scholars put at between 160 and 185 copies, about three-quarters of them on paper and the rest on vellum.

The printer changed the work as it went: the page grew from 40 lines to 42, an oil-based ink replaced the water-based inks of scribes, and headings and decoration were left for rubricators and illuminators to add by hand.
Forty-nine copies survive in at least substantial portion, together with fragments that probably represent about another 16 copies, and the book has long been counted among the world's most valuable.
dyk: The first pages printed had 40 lines each. After the page grew to 42 lines, apparently to save paper, the pages already printed had to be set again, so that two distinct settings exist in parts of both volumes.
ev: Preparation of the Bible probably begins soon after this date
The 31-line Indulgence, the first precisely datable print by Gutenberg, certainly exists by 22 October
The future Pope Pius II writes that he has seen pages of the Bible displayed at Frankfurt to promote the edition
The copy with the earliest visible print date is marked 15 August
The first Gutenberg Bible reaches North America; it is now in the New York Public Library
The New York dealer Gabriel Wells dismantles a damaged copy and sells its leaves as the Noble Fragments
The last sale of a complete Gutenberg Bible takes place
A copy stolen from Moscow State University in 2009 is recovered in an FSB sting operation

sections.origins:
The Gutenberg Bible is an edition of the Vulgate, the Latin translation of the Hebrew Bible, or Old Testament, and the Greek New Testament made by St Jerome. Its text contains emendations from the Parisian Bible tradition and further divergences. Johannes Gutenberg printed it at Mainz, in the Holy Roman Empire and the present-day Germany, in the 1450s.

It is unlikely that any of Gutenberg's early publications bore his name. The initial expense of press equipment and materials, and of the work to be done before the Bible was ready for sale, suggests that he may have started with more lucrative texts. These included several religious documents, a German poem and some editions of Aelius Donatus's Ars Grammatica, a popular Latin grammar school book.

Preparation of the Bible probably began soon after 1450, and the first finished copies were available in 1454 or 1455. It is not known exactly how long the printing took. The first precisely datable piece of printing is Gutenberg's 31-line Indulgence, which certainly existed by 22 October 1454. The 36-line Bible, said to be the second printed Bible, is also sometimes called a Gutenberg Bible, but may be the work of another printer.
sections.content:
The book is the Latin Bible in full, set in the blackletter type styles known as Textualis (Textura) and Schwabacher. Textura takes its name from the texture of the printed page, straight vertical strokes combined with horizontal lines that give the impression of a woven structure. Gutenberg already used justification, a vertical alignment at both the left and right-hand sides of the column. To achieve it he used characters of narrower widths, added extra spaces around punctuation and varied the widths of the spaces around words.

A single complete copy has 1,288 pages, usually bound in two volumes, with the first volume ending with the Book of Psalms. Each page has 42 lines, apart from the first ones printed. The pages were designed with spacious margins, which left room for decoration added by hand. Initially the rubrics, the headings before each book of the Bible, were printed, but this practice was quickly abandoned at an unknown date, and gaps were left for them to be added by hand. A guide to the text to be added to each page, printed for the use of rubricators, survives.

Most copies were divided into two volumes. Copies on vellum were heavier and for this reason were sometimes bound in three or four volumes. Nine copies keep fifteenth-century bindings, most of them made in Mainz or Erfurt.
sections.making:
Each sheet of paper was dampened before printing to improve ink absorption and was then pressed onto an inked surface of movable type. The type was re-inked after each sheet, and once the work was finished it was cleaned and redistributed into type cases. The method is a form of relief printing. Gutenberg developed an oil-based ink, primarily carbon with a high metallic content in which copper, lead and titanium predominate. The British Library's Kristian Jensen described it as a varnish rather than an ink, since water-based scribes' inks would run off metal type.

Every unique character needed a piece of master type, and with capitals, lower-case letters, punctuation marks and ligatures the Bible needed a set of 290 master characters. It seems probable that six pages, containing 15,600 characters altogether, were set at any one moment. The paper was folded after printing, and typically five folded sheets, or twenty printed pages, formed a section called a quinternion. The linen paper is thought to have been imported from Caselle in Piedmont, Italy, from its watermarks.

Part-way through, the number of lines was raised from 40 to 42 by narrowing the space between lines, presumably to save paper, and the print run was increased, so that pages already printed had to be set again.
sections.reception:
The Bible seems to have sold out immediately, with some early purchases made as far away as England and possibly Sweden and Hungary. At least some copies sold for 30 florins, equivalent to about 100 grams of gold and about three years' wages for a clerk. This made them significantly cheaper than manuscript Bibles, yet most students, priests and other people of moderate income could not have afforded them. It is assumed that most were sold to monasteries, universities and particularly wealthy individuals. Only one copy is known to have been privately owned in the fifteenth century.

Some copies were used for communal readings in monastery refectories, a few were certainly used for study, and others may have been kept for display. Kristian Jensen suggests that many were bought by wealthy and pious laymen for donation to religious institutions. The amount of decoration presumably depended on what each buyer could pay: some copies were never decorated, and vellum copies, which were more expensive, tend to be more highly decorated, although the vellum copy in the British Library has none. The place of decoration is known or inferred for about 30 copies; 13 of them may have been decorated in Mainz, while others were worked on as far away as London.
sections.survival:
Estimates of the print run vary. The letter of 1455 cites sources for both 158 and 180 copies, and scholars today think the surviving copies suggest between 160 and 185. Forty-nine copies are known in at least substantial portion, and fragments, some as small as a single leaf, probably represent about another 16 copies. Many fragments survive because they were used in the bindings of later books. Nine copies keep their fifteenth-century bindings, most made in Mainz or Erfurt. All copies seem to have stayed in Europe until the first reached North America in 1847.

Several long-lost copies were discovered in the twentieth century, which improved the understanding of how the Bible was produced and distributed. Some copies were broken up. In 1921 the dealer Gabriel Wells dismantled a damaged copy and sold the leaves as Noble Fragments, and in 1953 Charles Scribner's Sons dismembered a damaged paper copy of volume II, whose New Testament is now at Indiana University.

The New York General Theological Seminary's copy had a forged leaf of the Book of Ezekiel. A genuine leaf from a broken-up second volume replaced it in 1953, and the matching first volume of that copy was later found at Mons, Belgium. A two-volume paper copy was stolen from Moscow State University in 2009 and recovered in 2013.
sections.legacy:
The Gutenberg Bible marked the start of what is called the Gutenberg Revolution and of the age of printed books in the West, and it had a profound effect on the history of the printed book. In a legal paper written after its completion Gutenberg called the work Das Werk der Bücher, the work of the books. He had introduced the printing press to Europe and made printing with movable type efficient enough for the mass production of entire books.

It also influenced later editions of the Bible. It provided the model for several, among them the 36-line Bible, Mentelin's Latin Bible and the first and third Eggestein Bibles. The third Eggestein Bible was set from the copy now in Cambridge University Library. It also influenced the Clementine edition of the Vulgate commissioned by the Papacy in the late sixteenth century. The 36-line Bible, said to be the second printed Bible, is sometimes also called a Gutenberg Bible but may be the work of another printer.

Many book-lovers have commented on the standards of its production, some describing it as one of the most beautiful books ever printed. A library's possession of a copy has been equated to keeping a trophy book. Keio University in Tokyo has made digital reproductions of Gutenberg Bibles.

summary: The Gutenberg Bible is Johannes Gutenberg's printed Latin Vulgate of the 1450s, made at Mainz with mass-produced metal type. Of a print run put at between 160 and 185 copies, 49 survive in at least substantial portion, and it marked the start of the age of printed books in the West.
notes: The article contradicts itself on complete copies: the lead says 21 of the 49 survivors are complete, the Surviving copies section says 25 (as of 2009). The count of complete copies is left out.

The 1978 sale price is given as US$2.4 million in Recent history and the Forgeries section says the Seminary copy sold for US$2.2 million in 1978; prices left out. The article does not say whether these are the same sale.
The 1456 event rests on the lead's 'earliest visible print date is marked as 15 August 1456'. Dates of the first finished copies are 1454 or 1455; start 1450 is 'soon after 1450'.

The article does not say how many pages are 40-line beyond 1-9 and 256-265 and its folio detail is left out; the section on lines says the first pages printed were reset to 42 lines, as in the article.

Section 'making' says 'about three years' wages' only in reception, as the article gives it. Left out: the Golden Ratio dispute over paper size, the Master of the Playing Cards speculation, the HUMI project's counts, current value estimates, and the list of fragment holdings beyond a general mention.
